extracted.intended_audience: researchers, funding policy analysts, and agency staff concerned with grant peer review and allocation (especially NIH/biomedical community)
extracted.subtask_description: Re-analysis of NIH R01 grants (1980–2008) assessing how well peer-review percentile scores predict subsequent grant productivity (publications and citations), focusing on grants with percentile scores of 20 or better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of number of reviewers / statistical precision
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of reviewers on grant panels is typically inadequate to provide statistical precision in scoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small reviewer sample sizes reduce precision of scoring and make rankings less reliable (citing Kaplan et al., 2008). Implication: panels should consider whether reviewer counts are sufficient to yield reproducible distinctions among applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-reviewer variability and disagreement about criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: There is considerable variation among reviewers' scores and disagreement regarding review criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High variance and inconsistent application of criteria across reviewers undermines reliability of scores (cites Mayo et al., Graves et al., Abdoul et al.). Monitoring and training on criteria could be necessary to reduce variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer bias influencing funding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical analysis has found evidence of reviewer bias that influenced a substantial fraction of funding outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Bayesian hierarchical model of NIH applications suggested reviewer bias could affect as much as ~25% of funding decisions (Johnson, 2008). Bias should be accounted for when interpreting score-based rankings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review discriminates flawed proposals from sound ones but not among meritorious applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review can separate extremely strong applications from those with serious flaws, but it has limited ability to predict which meritorious applications will be most productive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once applications are deemed meritorious (within competitive percentiles), reviewers struggle to stratify them by future productivity; thus fine-grained ranking within this set may be unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentile scores are a poor discriminator of subsequent productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: For the analyzed set of 102,740 grants with percentile scores ≤20, percentile ranking correlates only modestly with publication and citation productivity and is a weak predictor overall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported statistics: slope = −0.132 ± 0.005 publications per percentile and −9.6 ± 0.337 citations per percentile; r² = 0.0078, indicating very little variance explained. Policy implication: heavy reliance on percentile rank to select among meritorious proposals is not justified by predictive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Very limited predictive power in the critical 3–20 percentile range
rubrics_metrics.description: Although applications with scores of 2 or better showed significantly more citations, this effect did not extend to applications with scores of 3–20; within this range, productivity differences are minimal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because current paylines typically lie within this percentile range, the inability to discriminate within 3–20 is especially important for funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) shows near-random discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: The ROC analysis yields an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.54 for percentile score predicting citation productivity above the median, indicating performance barely above chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An AUC of 1.0 is perfect discrimination and 0.5 is random; 0.54 implies percentile-based ranking provides almost no useful discriminatory power for predicting high vs. low productivity in the studied subset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-learning/random-forest importance is negligible
rubrics_metrics.description: A random forest model found that percentile ranking accounted for only ~0.98% (~1%) of variance in citation productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-parametric modeling corroborates the weak predictive contribution of percentile scores; model residuals and low importance values support rethinking the weight given to percentiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of publications and citations as productivity metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Using publications and citations to measure grant productivity has known limitations and temporal/cohort effects that can confound analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation practices changed over time (citations per paper approximately doubled between 1980 and 2004), and more recent grants may both have better percentile scores and higher citation counts for reasons unrelated to reviewer discrimination. Analysts should correct for cohort/year effects when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-independence of percentile scores and productivity due to funding timing and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentile scores and observed productivity may be linked through funding timing and administrative choices (e.g., exceptions, late-year funding, budget reductions) rather than reviewer discrimination alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grants funded despite scoring worse than the payline are often funded later in the fiscal year and may suffer budget cuts that reduce productivity; GAO reported ~13% of R01s were exceptions in 2003–2007. Analyses should consider these administrative confounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to limit fine-grained ranking and consider randomization within top tier
rubrics_metrics.description: Given reviewers' limited ability to discriminate among meritorious applications, a policy alternative is to identify the top ~20% of applications and allocate funding within this group by lottery or programmatic priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors suggest a modified lottery (cite Fang & Casadevall 2014) and note real-world precedent (New Zealand HRC Explorer Grants). This approach could save reviewer time and acknowledge inherent unpredictability of research outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concern that current paylines leave productive applications unfunded
rubrics_metrics.description: Current funding paylines are inadequate to fund many potentially productive applications, meaning substantial potential productivity may be left unfunded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because percentile scores poorly stratify meritorious applications, some highly productive projects receive poorer scores and are excluded by paylines; funding policy should account for this potential loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data and methodological transparency for replication
rubrics_metrics.description: Productivity was measured as number of publications acknowledging grant support within 5 years and citations through 2013; percentile scores were rounded to nearest whole number; analyses used parametric stats, ROC, and random forest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dataset was obtained from Li and Nakamura; restricted-access data are available via NIH Data Access Policy. Methods notes (time windows, rounding, software/packages used) are important when reproducing or extending the analysis.
